idiom_name: ScalaTest GivenWhenThen trait (given/when/then) in a suite
implementation_notes: Mixing org.scalatest.GivenWhenThen into a suite adds given/when/then/and methods that take a description and forward it to the reporter, so the beats appear in the test output as well as in the code; assertions come from Assertions (assert, assertResult) or Matchers (shouldBe). The classic fixture class becomes a suite class mixing in a style trait plus fixture traits (BeforeAndAfterEach), and because the clauses only inform the reporter they behave like richly reported comments.
pitfalls: The given/when/then clauses do not scope anything: a value defined in a When block is still in scope at Then, so a missing arrange step compiles and fails later with an unrelated error.
Style and fixture traits are mixed in, and mixin order decides which withFixture implementation wins - the wrong linearisation silently skips BeforeAndAfterEach setup.
Suites may run tests in parallel (sbt parallelExecution), so a mutable fixture shared across tests is a race unless each test arranges its own state.

variants.name: MUnit FunSuite test() with assertEquals
variants.idiom_name: MUnit FunSuite test blocks with assertEquals/assert
variants.implementation_notes: MUnit keeps the suite minimal: declare test(name) { ... } inside a FunSuite, arrange with ordinary vals on the suite or a constructor helper, perform one call as the act, and assert with assertEquals/assert, which print a diff of obtained versus expected. There is no fixture class to configure, so the xUnit structure is replaced by a function plus ordinary values, and asynchronous bodies returning Future are awaited by the framework.
pitfalls: assertEquals(obtained, expected) takes the obtained value first - the opposite of assertResult - and the diff is annotated with the operands, so swapped arguments read as a backwards failure.
An async body that constructs a Future without returning it passes immediately; the docs demonstrate this with a lazy future whose body is never evaluated.
MUnit does not run individual tests in parallel, but sbt parallelises suites, so a shared object mutated by two suites is still a race.
